You are shown a snapshot of US macroeconomic and market data as it was known at the end of one month between 2007 and 2026.

Estimate which month the snapshot describes. Use only the figures supplied plus your general knowledge of economic history.

Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"year": yyyy, "month": m, "confidence": c, "cues": ["...", "..."]}
Rules: year is an integer from 2007 to 2026; month is an integer from 1 to 12; c in [0, 1] is your confidence that the guess is within 6 months of the truth; 1 to 3 short cues citing the inputs.
text:
The unemployment rate is very low relative to its 3-year history and has fallen sharply, while payrolls are strong. The 2-year yield is very high, up 1.5 over 3 months and 12 months, and the policy rate is only slightly below average. That points to a hiking cycle or an expectations surge. The spread is slightly positive and falling.

Candidate periods: early 2022, mid-2022 and late 2016 are all possible. Late 2016 to early 2017 fits the 2-year yield surge after the election, but a 36-month window then would include a period of very low rates, which would make the policy rate z-score positive rather than -0.5. Early 2022 fits better: unemployment is falling fast (-2.0), payrolls are strong, and the 2-year yield is surging. But CPI z-scores near 0 do not fit early 2022, since inflation was then very high against the trailing 36 months.

Another option is 2018, when unemployment was low, the 2-year yield was high, the policy rate was rising, and CPI was around average. In 2018 the policy rate z-score would be high, though. The 2-year yield z +3 with a policy rate of -0.5 suggests the policy rate lags the market, so the market is pricing hikes.

Consider late 2023 or early 2024: unemployment was low, but the 36-month window would include 2021, when rates were near 0, so the policy rate z would be high. That does not fit.

Consider 2026 or late 2025: the window would cover 2023-2025, where the policy rate was high, and a -0.5 z fits after cuts. But a 2-year yield at +3 does not fit.

Consider 2022 more carefully. In March 2022 the window of 2019-2022 had a policy rate average of about 1%, and the rate then was 0.33%, so z was around -0.5. The 2-year yield jumped from 0.7% to 2.3% by March 2022, giving a z of +3. The 10-year was +1. The spread was falling. Unemployment fell from 6% to 3.6%, which is -2. Payrolls were +2. IP was strong. The VIX of -0.5 does not fit, and the CPI z of 0 is questionable since the window included the 2019-2020 low-inflation period, but CPI z would still be high. Equity returns around zero over 3 to 12 months, with a 1m return of -1, fit March-April 2022. The Baa spread z of -2 is odd, but possible.

I'll go with March 2022.
